pages.tldr: Enter the amount borrowed, the rate and the term. You get the monthly payment, the total interest, and — the number most calculators bury — what happens if you overpay. £250,000 at 4.5% over 25 years is £1,389.58 a month, with £166,874 of interest over the loan.
steps: Amount borrowed — price minus deposit, plus any fees you are rolling into the loan.
Rate and term — the rate on your deal and how long you want to be paying, not the maximum the lender offers.
Overpayment — try £100 or £200 a month and watch the term, not the payment. That single number usually decides whether overpaying is worth it.
pages.worked:
Borrow £250,000 at 4.5% over 25 years (300 payments). The monthly rate is 0.045 ÷ 12 = 0.00375, and the standard repayment formula gives £1,389.58 a month. Over 25 years you repay £416,874 in total — £166,874 of it interest.

Stretch the same loan to 30 years and the payment falls to £1,266.71 — but total interest rises to £206,017. Five extra years costs roughly £39,000 for a £123-a-month saving.

Overpay £200 a month on the 25-year loan and it clears in about 20 years instead of 25, saving roughly £38,500 in interest. Overpayments cut the term, not the payment.
pages.caveat: Not advice. This models fixed-rate, capital-and-interest repayment. It does not know your credit file, arrangement fees, or what rates will do when your fix ends. For decisions that matter, speak to a qualified mortgage adviser — and read the full guide to how mortgages work.
pages.limits_heading: What this calculator does not do
limits: Reversion rates. Most UK deals fix for 2–5 years then revert to the lender's variable rate. The payment shown is for the rate you enter.
Fees and charges. Arrangement fees, valuation fees and early-repayment charges are not in the number unless you add them to the amount borrowed.
Affordability. What you can borrow is the lender's decision (income multiples, stress tests, credit history) — this tool answers what a given loan costs, not whether you will get it.

faq.q: How is a UK mortgage payment calculated?
faq.a: Monthly payment = P × r × (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1), where P is the loan amount, r is the monthly rate (annual rate ÷ 12) and n is the number of monthly payments. On £250,000 at 4.5% over 25 years that is £1,389.58 a month.

faq.q: Do overpayments reduce my payment or my term?
faq.a: The term. Overpaying £200 a month on a £250,000 loan at 4.5% clears it in about 20 years instead of 25 and saves roughly £38,500 in interest. Most UK lenders allow 10% overpayment a year without charge during the fix.

faq.q: How much interest do I pay over the life of the loan?
faq.a: More than most summaries admit. £250,000 at 4.5% over 25 years costs £166,874 in interest; stretching to 30 years drops the payment by £123 a month but adds about £39,000 of interest.

faq.q: Is this mortgage advice?
faq.a: No. This is a calculator, not advice. It models fixed-rate capital-and-interest repayment; it does not know your credit file, the fees, or what rates will do next. For decisions that matter, speak to a qualified mortgage adviser.

pages.tldr: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. At 80 kg and 1.75 m that is 26.1 — the overweight band (25–29.9). Healthy is 18.5–24.9.
steps: Height and weight — metric or imperial, whichever you know.
Read the band, not just the number — 26.1 means little until you see it sits in 25–29.9 (overweight).
Check the healthy range for your height — at 1.75 m it is roughly 56.7–76.3 kg. The tool shows yours.
pages.worked: Weight 80 kg, height 1.75 m. Square the height: 1.75² = 3.0625. Divide: 80 ÷ 3.0625 = 26.1. Against the WHO bands — under 18.5 underweight, 18.5–24.9 healthy, 25–29.9 overweight, 30+ obese — that is overweight, about 3.8 kg above the top of the healthy range for this height.
pages.caveat: A screening tool, not a diagnosis. BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, and it says nothing about where fat sits — which matters more than the total. If a number here worries you, talk to a clinician, and read what BMI actually measures.
limits: Muscle. A muscular build scores overweight or obese with very little body fat. Athletes should look at body-fat estimates and waist measurement instead.
Fat distribution. Waist circumference predicts risk better than BMI alone — the NHS flags 94 cm+ for men and 80 cm+ for women as take-action levels.
Children, pregnancy, old age. Children use percentile charts, not adult bands; pregnancy and age-related muscle loss both break the standard interpretation.

faq.q: How is BMI calculated?
faq.a: BMI = weight in kilograms ÷ height in metres squared. At 80 kg and 1.75 m: 80 ÷ 3.0625 = 26.1, which sits in the overweight band (25–29.9).

faq.q: What is a healthy BMI?
faq.a: The WHO healthy range is 18.5–24.9. For someone 1.75 m tall that is roughly 56.7–76.3 kg. Below 18.5 is underweight, 25–29.9 overweight, 30 and above obese.

faq.q: Why is BMI wrong for athletes?
faq.a: BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. A muscular rugby player can score overweight or obese with very little body fat. It is a population screening tool, not a body-composition scan — waist measurement and body-fat estimates fill the gap.

faq.q: Can children use this BMI calculator?
faq.a: Not directly. Children's BMI is interpreted against age-and-sex percentile charts, not adult bands. This tool uses the adult WHO bands only.

pages.lede: What savings really grow to — lump sums, monthly top-ups, and the 10-, 20- and 30-year horizons where compounding does its serious work. Free, in-browser, no sign-up.
pages.tldr: £10,000 at 7% for 20 years grows to £38,696.84 untouched. Add £500 a month and it becomes £300,850.72 — you paid in £130,000 and compounding did the other £170,851.
steps: Starting amount and rate — what you have now and the annual return you want to model. Try 4% for cautious, 7% for the long-run stock-market average often quoted.
Monthly top-up — the number that matters most. Small regular additions beat clever rate-picking over long horizons.
Years — run 10, 20 and 30 side by side. The gap between them is the whole argument for starting now.
pages.worked:
Start with £10,000 at 7%, compounded yearly, for 20 years, no top-ups. The formula is A = P(1 + r)^t: £10,000 × 1.07^20 = £10,000 × 3.8697 = £38,696.84. Nearly quadrupled, while you did nothing.

Now add £500 every month. The lump sum still grows to £38,696.84 — and the 240 monthly payments, each compounding for whatever is left of the 20 years, add about £262,154 on top, for £300,850.72 total. You contributed £130,000. The market calendar contributed the rest.

The shortcut the example hides: the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the rate for the doubling time — at 7%, money doubles every 10.3 years. Two doublings in 20 years is roughly ×4, which is exactly what the formula says.
pages.caveat: Arithmetic, not advice. This assumes a smooth fixed return every year, which no real investment delivers, and it ignores inflation, tax and fees. For decisions that matter, speak to a qualified financial adviser — and read why compound growth is magic.
limits: Inflation. £300,000 in 20 years buys less than £300,000 today. At 2.5% inflation it buys what about £183,000 buys now. Real return is what matters.
Tax wrappers. The same money inside an ISA (£20,000 a year allowance) keeps all of it; outside one, interest and gains may be taxed.
Volatility and fees. Real returns lurch; a 1% annual fee quietly eats roughly a quarter of a 30-year return. Model 7% if you expect 8% and pay 1%.

faq.q: What is the compound interest formula?
faq.a: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt): principal × (1 + rate ÷ compounds-per-year) ^ (compounds × years). £10,000 at 7% compounded yearly for 20 years is £10,000 × 1.07^20 = £38,696.84.

faq.q: What is the rule of 72?
faq.a: Divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate doubling time. At 7%, money doubles in about 10.3 years. It breaks down above ~15% and ignores contributions, but it is right where it matters.

faq.q: How much does £500 a month grow to?
faq.a: £500 a month for 20 years at 7% — on top of a £10,000 start — grows to about £300,851. You paid in £130,000; compounding did the other £170,851. Time does more work than the monthly amount.

faq.q: Is this financial advice?
faq.a: No. This is arithmetic, not advice. It assumes a smooth fixed return every year, which no real investment delivers, and it ignores inflation, tax and fees. For decisions that matter, speak to a qualified financial adviser.

faq.q: How is a monthly loan payment calculated?
faq.a: Monthly payment = P × i × (1+i)^n / ((1+i)^n − 1), where P is the amount borrowed, i is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12) and n is the number of payments. On {{amount}} at {{rate}}% over {{years}} years that is {{payment}} a month.

faq.q: Does overpaying a loan actually save money?
faq.a: Yes, and the saving comes from the term rather than the payment. Adding {{extra}} a month to {{amount}} at {{rate}}% clears it in about {{term_with_extra}} years instead of {{years}} and saves roughly {{interest_saved}} in interest. The monthly payment itself usually stays the same.

faq.q: What is the difference between the interest rate and the APR?
faq.a: The rate is what you are charged on the balance. The APR also folds in most fees and the timing of payments, so it is the honest number for comparing two offers — a lower rate with a big arrangement fee can cost more than a higher rate without one.

faq.q: Why is most of my early payment interest rather than debt?
faq.a: Interest is charged on the balance, and early on the balance is still close to the full amount. On {{amount}} at {{rate}}% the first month's interest is {{first_interest}} of the {{payment}} payment; by the final year almost all of it is principal. Overpaying early avoids interest that would otherwise be charged for years.

faq.q: Will my bank quote the same monthly payment?
faq.a: Close, but not always identical — lenders round differently, count the first payment from a different date, or charge interest daily rather than monthly. Use this for the decision and the lender's documents for the exact figure.

pages.schema_description: Free BMR calculator using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, with activity multipliers for estimated daily energy needs. Runs in your browser.
pages.og_title: BMR Calculator — Mifflin-St Jeor, With Activity Levels
pages.og_description: Resting energy needs from weight, height, age and sex — plus what that means at each activity level. No sign-up, no ads.
pages.twitter_description: Basal metabolic rate, with the activity multipliers that turn it into a daily estimate.
pages.lede: The energy your body uses at rest, worked out from weight, height, age and sex — then multiplied by activity to reach a daily figure. An estimate from a published equation, not a prescription.
pages.tldr: A 30-year-old man at {{kg}} kg and {{cm}} cm has a BMR of about {{bmr_male}} kcal a day ({{bmr_female}} for a woman of the same height and weight). Multiply by activity — 1.55 for moderate exercise three to five days a week — and the daily estimate is roughly {{tdee_moderate}} kcal.
steps: Weight and height — measured, not remembered. The equation is sensitive to both, and old numbers are the most common source of a figure that looks wrong.
Age — the equation subtracts 5 kcal a day for every year, because resting energy use falls slowly with age.
Sex — the constants differ (the female term is about 166 kcal lower for the same body), so this is not a cosmetic toggle.
Activity level — the multiplier that turns a resting figure into a daily one, and the input most people get wrong by choosing who they wish they were rather than what an average week looks like.
pages.worked:
The tool uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, currently the recommended estimate for healthy adults: men 10w + 6.25h − 5a + 5, women 10w + 6.25h − 5a − 161, with weight in kilograms, height in centimetres and age in years.

For a {{age}}-year-old man at {{kg}} kg and {{cm}} cm: (10 × {{kg}}) + (6.25 × {{cm}}) − (5 × {{age}}) + 5 = {{bmr_male}} kcal a day at complete rest. The same person as a woman would be {{bmr_female}} kcal — the two equations differ by a constant, not by a percentage.

That resting figure is not what you burn in a day. Multiply by activity: sedentary 1.2 gives {{tdee_sedentary}} kcal, light exercise 1.375 gives {{tdee_light}}, moderate 1.55 gives {{tdee_moderate}}, very active 1.725 gives {{tdee_active}} and an athlete training hard around a physical job (1.9) gives {{tdee_athlete}}. The same body, a range of about 1,150 kcal a day, decided entirely by movement.
pages.caveat: An estimate, not medical advice or a diet plan. BMR equations describe populations, not people: individual results commonly differ by around 10%, and more with thyroid conditions, pregnancy, medication or significant muscle mass. If you are managing a health condition or an eating disorder, talk to a clinician or dietitian — a number from a web page is the wrong starting point.
pages.limits_heading: What a BMR number cannot know
limits: Body composition. Two people at {{kg}} kg differ in how much of that is muscle, and muscle burns more at rest than fat does. The equation only sees the total.
Medical context. Illness, recovery, some medications and thyroid conditions move resting energy use well outside the normal range.
Who the formula was built from. Mifflin-St Jeor was derived from a specific adult population; it is less accurate at the extremes of height, weight and age.
Your actual week. The multiplier is a blunt average. A day of desk work and a day of hill walking are not 1.55 each.

faq.q: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
faq.a: BMR is what you would burn lying still all day. TDEE (total daily energy expenditure) is BMR multiplied by an activity factor — the calories you actually use in a normal week. On the worked example here, {{bmr_male}} kcal at rest becomes about {{tdee_moderate}} kcal at moderate activity.

faq.q: Which BMR formula does this calculator use?
faq.a: Mifflin-St Jeor, the equation most often recommended for healthy adults: 10 × weight in kg, plus 6.25 × height in cm, minus 5 × age, plus 5 for men or minus 161 for women. Older Harris-Benedict equations tend to overestimate by around 5%.

faq.q: How accurate is a BMR estimate?
faq.a: Expect roughly ±10% against a laboratory measurement for most healthy adults, and wider at the extremes of body size or age. It is accurate enough to plan around and not accurate enough to treat as a measurement of you.

faq.q: Does building muscle change my BMR?
faq.a: Yes, modestly. Muscle is metabolically active at rest, so adding lean mass raises resting energy use — but the widely repeated figure of 50 extra calories per pound of muscle is far too high. Realistic changes are real and small.

faq.q: Should I eat to my BMR or my TDEE?
faq.a: That is a decision for you and, ideally, a clinician or dietitian — not for a calculator. This page tells you what your body uses, nothing about what you should eat. Anyone managing a health condition or disordered eating should disregard the number entirely and speak to a professional.

pages.og_description: Percentages with the working shown: percent of, increase, decrease, change and reverse. No sign-up, no ads.
pages.twitter_description: Percent of, increase, decrease, change and reverse percentages — with the working shown.
pages.lede: Percentages, with the working visible: a percentage of a number, an increase or decrease, the change between two numbers, and the reverse case where you know the result and need the original. Everything runs in your browser.
pages.tldr: {{percent}}% of {{value}} is {{of}}. Increase {{value}} by {{percent}}% and you get {{increase}}; decrease it and you get {{decrease}}. Going from {{from}} to {{to}} is a {{change_pct}}% increase.
steps: Pick the mode first — the seven modes answer genuinely different questions, and the most common percentage mistake is answering the wrong one confidently.
Basic percentage — X% of Y, the everyday case such as a tip, a discount or a tax rate.
Increase or decrease — apply a percentage change to a value, forwards.
What percentage is X of Y — turn a score or a share into a percentage.
Percentage change — compare old and new values, for prices, metrics and results.
Reverse percentage — when you know the number after the change and need the number before it, such as removing VAT from a total.
pages.worked:
{{percent}}% of {{value}} is {{value}} × 0.15 = {{of}}. Once a percentage is a decimal, every other mode is the same arithmetic pointed in a different direction.

Increase: {{value}} × 1.15 = {{increase}}. Decrease: {{value}} × 0.85 = {{decrease}}. The multiplier is the whole trick — add or subtract the percentage from 1, then multiply once.

Change between two values: going from {{from}} to {{to}} is ({{to}} − {{from}}) ÷ {{from}} = 0.25, a {{change_pct}}% increase. Going back down from {{to}} to {{from}} is not a {{change_pct}}% fall — it is 20%, because the second calculation divides by a larger base. That asymmetry is the single most common percentage error in print.

Reverse: if a total includes 20% VAT and comes to £{{value}}, the price before VAT is not £{{value}} − 20%. It is 240 ÷ 1.2 = £200 — dividing out the multiplier rather than subtracting the tax.
pages.caveat: Arithmetic, not advice. Percentages are exact only when the inputs are. Discounts that stack, interest that compounds and averages of percentages all behave differently from the simple cases on this page — the calculator shows what a percentage means, not what a contract means.
limits: Stacked percentages do not add. 10% off then another 10% off is 19% off, not 20% — the second discount applies to the reduced price.
Percentage change is asymmetric. A 50% fall needs a 100% rise to get back, because the two changes use different bases.
Percentage points are not percent. A rate moving from 4% to 5% has risen by one percentage point, or 25% — both statements are true and they sound very different.
Averaging percentages. The average of 50% and 100% is not 75% unless both cases have the same base size.

faq.q: How do I work out a percentage of a number?
faq.a: Turn the percentage into a decimal and multiply. {{percent}}% of {{value}} is {{value}} × 0.15 = {{of}}. For a quick mental estimate, 10% means moving the decimal point one place left, then scale from there.

faq.q: How do I reverse a percentage?
faq.a: Divide by the multiplier instead of subtracting the percentage. If £{{value}} includes 20% VAT, the pre-VAT price is {{value}} ÷ 1.2 = £200 — not £{{value}} minus 20%, which would give £192 and understate the tax.

faq.q: What is the difference between percent and percentage points?
faq.a: A move from 4% to 5% is one percentage point, and also a 25% increase. Percentages describe relative change; percentage points describe an absolute difference between two percentages. Mixing them is one of the most common errors in reporting.

faq.q: Why does a 50% fall need a 100% rise to recover?
faq.a: Because each change is measured against a different base. Falling from {{to}} to {{from}} divides by {{to}}; rising back divides by {{from}}. The base set by the changed value is smaller, so the same absolute move is a larger percentage.

faq.q: Does this calculator handle repeated percentage change?
faq.a: Yes, use the compound mode: applying the same percentage several times means raising the multiplier to a power. Two consecutive 10% increases are 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, a 21% rise, not 20%.

pages.worked:
Birth date: 15 March 1990. As-of: today. Counting forward: from 15 March 1990 to 15 March 2026 is exactly 36 years. From 15 March to 4 October is 6 months and 19 days, so the exact age is 36 years, 6 months and 19 days.

In total days that is roughly 13,352 days — or about 1,908 weeks. The number of days matters more than people expect: many legal and financial calculations (pension eligibility, insurance, statutory rights) count in days or months, not years.

Try a historical date: how old was someone born on 4 July 1976 on 1 January 2000? The answer is 23 years, 5 months and 28 days — not the "24" most people would round to.
pages.caveat: Calendar precision, not a legal determination. This calculator uses the standard Gregorian calendar and handles leap years correctly, but age for legal, pension or immigration purposes may be calculated differently depending on jurisdiction. For anything that matters, check the rules that apply to your situation.
pages.limits_heading: What this calculator does not account for
limits: Time zones and exact time of birth. A date-only calculator cannot know whether you were born at 11:59 pm or 12:01 am. For most purposes the date alone is enough; for some legal contexts the exact time matters.

Calendar systems. This uses the Gregorian calendar exclusively. Dates before 15 October 1582 (when the Gregorian calendar was adopted) are handled as proleptic Gregorian, which may differ from historical records.
Leap seconds and civil time adjustments. The calculator counts calendar days, not SI seconds. Historical changes to timekeeping (pre-1972 leap second irregularities, for example) are not modelled.

faq.q: How do you calculate exact age in years, months and days?
faq.a: Count full years from the birth date to the as-of date, then count remaining full months, then remaining days. Someone born 15 March 1990 counted on 4 October 2026: 36 full years (to 15 March 2026), then 6 full months (to 15 September), then 19 days — 36 years, 6 months and 19 days.

faq.q: Why is my exact age different from the age I tell people?
faq.a: Most people round down to the last birthday. Your exact age includes the months and days since that birthday. Someone who turned 36 in March is 36 years and several months old — the exact figure matters for insurance, pension eligibility and legal deadlines that count in months or days.

faq.q: Does this calculator handle leap years?
faq.a: Yes. Leap days are counted correctly, including the century rules (years divisible by 100 are not leap years unless also divisible by 400). Someone born on 29 February has a valid entry and the calculator counts correctly to non-leap-year as-of dates.

faq.q: Can I calculate age at a past or future date?
faq.a: Yes — the as-of date defaults to today but can be set to any date. Useful for retirement eligibility checks, historical research, or working out how old someone was on a specific day.

pages.title: Body Fat Calculator — US Navy Tape-Measure Method with Body Composition
pages.description: Free body fat calculator using the US Navy tape-measure method: enter neck, waist and hip measurements, get estimated body-fat percentage and fat-free mass. Private, in-browser, no sign-up.

pages.og_description: Free body fat calculator: tape-measure method with body composition. Private and in-browser — your measurements never leave your device.

pages.twitter_description: Free body fat calculator using the US Navy tape-measure method. Private, in-browser, no sign-up.
pages.lede: An estimate of body-fat percentage from tape measurements — neck, waist and (for women) hip — using the US Navy method. Not as accurate as a DEXA scan, but free, private and available right now in your browser.
pages.tldr: The US Navy method estimates body-fat percentage from neck circumference, waist circumference and height (plus hip for women). A man with a 37-inch waist, 15-inch neck and 70-inch height is estimated at roughly 19.5% body fat — within the fitness range for adult men.
steps: Height — measured, not remembered. Stand against a wall without shoes.
Neck — measure at the narrowest point, just below the Adam's apple. Keep the tape level and do not pull it tight.
Waist — at the navel for men, at the narrowest point for women. Measure after a normal exhale, not sucked in.
Hips (women only) — at the widest point of the hips.
Read the category, not just the number. The estimate has a margin of error; the category (essential fat, athletes, fitness, average, obese) is more useful than the decimal places.
pages.worked:
A man, 70 inches tall, 37-inch waist, 15-inch neck. The US Navy formula for men is: body fat % = 86.010 × log₁₀(waist − neck) − 70.041 × log₁₀(height) + 36.76.

Waist minus neck: 37 − 15 = 22 inches. log₁₀(22) = 1.3424, log₁₀(70) = 1.8451. So: 86.010 × 1.3424 − 70.041 × 1.8451 + 36.76 = 115.46 − 129.23 + 36.76 = approximately 19.5%.

For a woman at 64 inches tall, 29-inch waist, 13-inch neck, 38-inch hips: the formula uses waist + hip − neck. The result depends on all four tape measurements and height, which is why women need one extra measurement.
pages.caveat: An estimate from a formula, not a measurement. The US Navy method correlates with hydrostatic weighing but can differ by several percentage points, especially at the extremes of body size or for people who carry fat differently from the formula's assumptions. For clinical body composition, DEXA or hydrostatic weighing are the reference methods. If a number here concerns you, talk to a clinician.
pages.limits_heading: What a tape measure cannot tell you
limits: Fat distribution. This method gives a single percentage; it says nothing about where the fat sits. Visceral fat (around the organs) carries more health risk than subcutaneous fat, and this method cannot distinguish them.
Muscle mass changes. If you are building muscle and losing fat at the same time, the tape measurements may not move as fast as your body composition is changing.
Individual variation. The formula was derived from population data; individual error is commonly ±3–4 percentage points. Use it for trends over weeks, not for a single reading.
Not for children or pregnant women. The US Navy formula was developed for adults and is not validated for children, adolescents or pregnancy.

faq.q: How does the US Navy body fat method work?
faq.a: It estimates body-fat percentage from height, neck circumference and waist circumference (plus hip for women). The formula calculates the difference between waist and neck as a proxy for trunk fat, then adjusts for height. It was developed from comparison with hydrostatic weighing and correlates well for most adults.

faq.q: How accurate is a tape-measure body fat estimate?
faq.a: Expect roughly ±3–4 percentage points against a DEXA scan. It is accurate enough to track trends over time (which is what matters) and less accurate for a single reading. Measure under the same conditions each time — same time of day, same clothing, same tension on the tape.

faq.q: What is a healthy body fat percentage?
faq.a: For men: essential fat 2–5%, athletes 6–13%, fitness 14–17%, acceptable 18–24%, obese 25%+. For women: essential 10–13%, athletes 14–20%, fitness 21–24%, acceptable 25–31%, obese 32%+. These are population ranges — individual health depends on more than a single number.

faq.q: Why do I need to measure my neck?
faq.a: Neck circumference accounts for differences in frame size and upper-body muscle mass. A person with a thick neck and a 34-inch waist has a very different body composition from someone with a thin neck and the same waist measurement. Without the neck, the formula would overestimate body fat for muscular builds.

faq.q: Is body fat percentage better than BMI?
faq.a: They measure different things. BMI is a screening tool based on height and weight; body fat percentage tries to measure actual fat mass. BMI is faster and needs no measurements; body fat is more informative for individuals, especially muscular people whom BMI misclassifies. Neither is a diagnosis.

pages.title: WCAG Contrast Checker — Text and UI Colour Accessibility Ratio
pages.description: Free WCAG contrast checker: enter foreground and background colours, get the contrast ratio, AA and AAA pass/fail for normal text, large text and UI components. Runs in your browser — no sign-up.

pages.og_description: Free WCAG contrast checker: foreground vs background, AA and AAA compliance. No sign-up, no ads.
pages.twitter_title: WCAG Contrast Checker — Accessibility Colour Ratio
pages.twitter_description: Free WCAG contrast checker: contrast ratio, AA and AAA pass/fail. No sign-up, no ads.
pages.lede: Check whether two colours meet the WCAG 2.1 contrast requirements — foreground text on background, for normal text, large text and UI components. Enter hex codes or pick colours; the ratio and pass/fail results update live.
pages.tldr: Enter a foreground and background colour. The tool calculates the WCAG 2.1 contrast ratio and tells you whether the combination passes AA (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) and AAA (7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively). Black on white is 21:1 — the maximum. White on white is 1:1 — invisible.
steps: Foreground colour — the text or icon colour. Enter a hex code (#ffffff) or use the colour picker.
Background colour — what the text sits on. If the background is an image or gradient, sample the lightest or darkest area that text crosses.

Read the ratio and the compliance badges. AA is the legal minimum in most accessibility regulations; AAA is the higher standard. Normal text needs 4.5:1 (AA) or 7:1 (AAA); text at 18pt or 14pt bold and above needs 3:1 (AA) or 4.5:1 (AAA).
Check UI components too. WCAG 2.1 requires 3:1 for graphical objects and UI components (icons, form borders, focus indicators) — the tool reports this as well.
pages.worked:
Foreground: #1a1a2e (dark navy). Background: #f5f5f5 (off-white). The tool computes the relative luminance of each colour using the WCAG formula: L = 0.2126×R + 0.7152×G + 0.0722×B (after linearising the sRGB values).

The lighter colour's luminance plus 0.05, divided by the darker colour's luminance plus 0.05, gives the ratio. For #1a1a2e on #f5f5f5 the ratio is approximately 15.1:1 — a comfortable pass at every WCAG level: AAA for normal text (needs 7:1), AAA for large text (needs 4.5:1), and well above the 3:1 threshold for UI components.

Now try #777777 on #ffffff: the ratio is about 4.48:1 — a narrow fail for AA normal text (needs 4.5:1) but a pass for large text and UI components. This is the kind of near-miss that catches designers in audits.
pages.caveat: A tool for checking contrast, not a full accessibility audit. Colour contrast is one of the most common WCAG failures, but accessibility is much wider: keyboard navigation, screen reader semantics, focus management, motion sensitivity and content structure all matter. This tool checks one criterion (WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.3 and 1.4.11) thoroughly — a screening tool that points at a problem, not a diagnosis of one.
pages.limits_heading: What contrast ratio alone cannot tell you
limits: Font rendering and anti-aliasing. The ratio is a mathematical property of the two colours; it does not account for how a particular font renders at a particular size on a particular screen. Thin fonts at small sizes need higher contrast than the minimum to be legible in practice.
Background images and gradients. If text sits on a photo or gradient, the effective contrast varies across the text. Sample the worst case, not the best.
Cognitive accessibility. High contrast helps, but clear language, consistent layout and predictable interactions matter at least as much for many users.
Colour is not the only signal. WCAG 1.4.1 requires that colour is not the sole means of conveying information. A green/red pass/fail needs a text label or icon as well.

faq.q: What is the WCAG contrast ratio?
faq.a: The contrast ratio measures the difference in perceived brightness between two colours, ranging from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). The WCAG 2.1 guidelines require 4.5:1 for normal-sized text (AA), 3:1 for large text (AA), 7:1 for normal text (AAA) and 4.5:1 for large text (AAA).

faq.q: What counts as large text for WCAG?
faq.a: Text that is at least 18pt (24px) or at least 14pt (18.66px) bold. Large text has a lower contrast requirement (3:1 for AA instead of 4.5:1) because larger characters are easier to read at lower contrast. Body text at 16px is normal text, not large.

faq.q: Do I need to meet AAA or is AA enough?
faq.a: AA is the minimum required by most accessibility laws (the Equality Act in the UK, the ADA in the US, the European Accessibility Act). AAA is the enhanced standard and is recommended where practical, but the guidelines do not require AAA for all content — it is aspirational for many organisations.

faq.q: How is the contrast ratio calculated?
faq.a: The WCAG formula converts each colour's sRGB values to linear light, computes a relative luminance (L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B), then divides the lighter luminance plus 0.05 by the darker luminance plus 0.05. The result is a ratio from 1:1 to 21:1.

pages.lede: Generate a QR code that connects any phone or laptop to your Wi-Fi network in one scan — no typing the password, no spelling it out at the door. Your network credentials stay in your browser and are never sent anywhere.
pages.tldr: Enter your Wi-Fi network name (SSID) and password. The tool generates a standard Wi-Fi QR code that any modern phone camera can scan to connect instantly. Your credentials are processed entirely in your browser — nothing is sent to a server.
steps: Network name (SSID) — exactly as it appears in your Wi-Fi settings, including capitalisation and spaces.
Password — the current Wi-Fi password. Special characters are encoded correctly.
Security type — WPA/WPA2 is the default and covers most home networks. WEP and open networks are also supported but WEP is rare and insecure.
Hidden network — tick this if your network does not broadcast its SSID. The QR code will include the H: flag so the phone knows to look for it.
Print or share the QR code. Guests scan it with their phone camera and connect without typing anything.
pages.worked:
Network: MyHomeWiFi, password: correcthorse99, security: WPA/WPA2. The tool encodes this into the standard Wi-Fi QR format: WIFI:T:WPA;S:MyHomeWiFi;P:correcthorse99;;

That string becomes a QR code. Any iPhone (iOS 11+) or Android phone (10+) with a camera app that reads QR codes will recognise the WIFI: prefix and offer to connect — no app installation, no typing. The password is embedded in the QR code itself, which is why you should only display this code where you trust the visitors.

A hidden network adds H:true to the string. Without it, a phone will try to connect to a visible network of that name and fail silently if the network is hidden.
pages.caveat: The QR code contains your password in plain text. Anyone who scans it can read the password. Print it for trusted visitors only — do not put it on a public-facing window, a social media post or a business listing unless you intend the network to be public. For guest access, most routers support a separate guest network with its own password. It is a convenience for sharing access, not advice on how to secure your network.
pages.limits_heading: What to know before you print
limits: Security of the QR code itself. The QR code is a plain encoding of your SSID and password. If you photograph or share the code image, you are sharing your password. Treat it like a written password.

Special characters in SSID or password. If your network name or password contains a semicolon, comma, backslash, double quote or colon, the tool encodes them with a backslash escape as the Wi-Fi QR specification requires. Most phone cameras handle this correctly; a few older models do not.

Enterprise networks (WPA2-Enterprise / 802.1X). These use a username and password or certificate, not a shared passphrase. The standard Wi-Fi QR format does not support enterprise authentication — this tool is for home and small-office WPA2-Personal networks.
Router compatibility. Some ISPs lock the SSID or password; if you change either, the QR code needs regenerating. The tool does not store previous codes.

faq.q: How does a Wi-Fi QR code work?
faq.a: The QR code encodes a string in the format WIFI:T:WPA;S:networkname;P:password;;. When a phone camera scans it, the operating system recognises the WIFI: prefix and offers to connect to that network with the stored credentials — no app installation or manual entry needed.

faq.q: Is my Wi-Fi password safe when I generate a QR code?
faq.a: In this tool, yes — the QR code is generated entirely in your browser. Your password is never sent to a server. However, the QR code itself contains the password in readable form, so anyone who scans it (or photographs the printed code) can read it. Display the code only where you trust the audience.

faq.q: Which phones can scan Wi-Fi QR codes?
faq.a: iPhones running iOS 11 or later (using the built-in Camera app) and most Android phones running Android 10 or later (using the camera or Google Lens). On older phones, a dedicated QR scanner app may be needed.

faq.q: Can I use this for a guest network?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the best uses. Generate a separate QR code for your guest network and print it near the door. Guests connect without you spelling out the password, and you can change the guest password whenever you like — just regenerate the code.
